seriesTitle: The Lantern Mender of Pell Street
title: Dark Lamps
blurb: Emrys crosses the water to ask who lit the lamps on Flood Night. A drowned bargeman's lantern answers part of it.

blocks.text: Emrys Vale stood at the edge of the Pell Street steps with the toes of his good boots over the water, breathing like a man counting.
Ada stood beside him. Below them the canal moved, brown and patient, and slapped the bottom step.
"You don't have to," she said.
"For the record," said Emrys, "I do." He did not look away from the water. "Someone pulled me out of this. When I was a boy. I have never known who. I would like to."
Out on the canal, oars creaked towards them. Dip. Creak. Dip.

She had shown him the note at first bell, flat on the shop bench: the brown tape, the torn nib, *Ask who lit the lamps on Flood Night.* He had read it three times, then folded his spectacles and said, "The lower quay. I want to see it from the water." And then he had walked down the steps, for the first time in some years, and stopped.
The flat black boat bumped the step. Old Nobody shipped his oars and smiled up at them.
"Morning. What's your name?"
"Ada."
"Ada." He nodded, pleased. "And yours, sir?"
"Emrys Vale."
"Vale." Barnaby held out a long creased hand. "Mind the middle. She rocks."
Emrys took the hand and stepped down into the boat as if into a cold bath, and sat very straight with both fists on his knees. Ada sat beside him. Neither of them mentioned it.

The lower quay came out of the mist slowly: the long stone lip, the weedy steps going down into the water, and the iron posts, one after another, each with its glass lamp, dark by day. Emrys counted them under his breath. Twenty-three.
"Twenty-three lamps," said Ada. "If they'd been lit, you could have seen every step on this quay from the water."
"Eleven people drowned within reach of those steps," said Emrys quietly.
Neither of them had said the next part aloud. He said it now.

"Eleven lines gone from my book. Eleven drowned." He took his spectacles off. "Whoever had the lamps that night has the best reason in Morrow Quay to want those eleven forgotten. That is not a note about lamps, Ada. It is a note about the Breaker."
The oars dripped. Barnaby hummed something with no tune to it.
"What's your name?" he asked Emrys, kindly.
Emrys went to the hall, where the records could be read from third bell to sixth. Ada went to find the lamplighter.

Hester's oil store was a low brick arch under the bridge, smelling of paraffin and onions. A pot sat on a little iron stove, muttering to itself, and Hester was stirring it in her black gloves, humming.
"There's my duck! You're thin. Sit."
"Hester. Who lit the lamps on the lower quay on Flood Night?"
The spoon went round once more. Then it stopped.
"Now where's a nice girl like you got a question like that?"
"An old note."

"Old notes." Hester laughed and ladled stew into a chipped bowl. "Roster went down with the flood, petal. Whole lot of it. Paper doesn't swim." She pushed the bowl across the barrel top. "Eat that. Mutton and barley. You've the look of someone who's been mending on an empty stomach."
"You'd have been new on the lamps then."
"Fifteen, love. I did what I was told and went where I was sent." She wiped the ladle on her apron. "A wick only burns what it's given. Is that too salty? Tell me if it's too salty."
It was not too salty. It was very good. Ada ate all of it, sitting on an upturned crate, with the canal knocking at the arch and Hester humming over the stove.
Fifteen. Ten years. Somewhere at the back of Ada's head a sum began to add itself up, and Ada, who always did the sum, put it down unfinished and asked for more bread.
At ninth bell she tipped Barnaby's tin out on the shop bench.

Most of it was canal glass: bottle green, brown, a blue that had once been medicine, all worn soft as soap. But under that, wrapped in a rag, were curved pieces, thick and faintly amber. Lantern glass. And they were warm, very slightly, the way a cup is warm a minute after somebody has put it down.
Nine of them. She turned each one over and laid them out by curve, edge to edge. Emrys sat at the end of the bench with the Register open and did not speak.
The readout came up pale gold over the pieces. GLASS. And beneath it, as she had known it would: INCOMPLETE.
A line of light ran through all nine, joining them, then ran off the last one across the bench and stopped, pointing at nothing. The bar came up empty, with its notch cut out of the far end.
"One missing," she said. "The last one. Again."
"Whose is it?"
"No idea. And nobody to ask leave of. Nobody can give leave for a man nobody remembers."
"Then for the record," said Emrys, "I am witnessing that you wished you could ask."
She set her fingertips to the first seam. The glass clicked. The wick hissed as it remembered it was a wick.

The bar crept. Her hands began to ache at the knuckles, then the wrists. She counted, low. At thirty-one the bar reached the notch and stopped there, full as it would go, and the secret came up through the glass like cold water.
Night. Rain coming sideways. Water over the lower quay, knee-deep and pulling.
Every lamp on the quay was dark. Light only far up the hill, and shouting.
She was standing on the quay steps, halfway down, in a big man's body, with one big hand locked round an iron ring in the wall. His breath came ragged. He was so cold. He was so afraid.
"Move," he said, in a deep, slow voice. "Move, Wendel."
He didn't.
At the far end of the quay the sluice gate roared, and above it the great head beam groaned like a ship. Then a long, splitting crack of timber.

A young man, Tobias, ten years younger and soaked to the skin, threw himself at a small dark-haired woman and shoved her hard. She went over the edge into the canal. The beam came down where she had been standing, across the quay, and took an iron lamp post with it.
Tobias, on the far side of the beam, could not see the water now. Wendel could.
She came up. Ines. Hair plastered flat, gasping. And beside her, in the black water, something small was going under: a boy, ten or so, in a coat too big for him.
Ines got a fist in his collar. She kicked. She swam him to the steps and shoved him up at them, at Wendel's feet.
"Take him!" Odile's voice, slower, lower. "Take him!"
Wendel did not let go of the ring.
The boy clawed his own way up the steps, past Wendel's boots, and was gone up the quay.
Ines's hand was on the bottom step. Then the water turned, and her hand was not.
"Can't," said Wendel, to nobody. "God help me. Can't."
The water came up over his boots. The memory ran out ragged, like a torn page, and at the torn edge, for half a breath, a dark glove, fingers closing.
Ada sat back. The lantern on the bench was whole except for a ragged gap low on one side, the size of a thumbnail. A small low flame burned in it, steady.
Emrys was looking at the Register.

On a blank line halfway down a page, soft brown ink was coming up out of the paper, old ink, not his: *Pike, Wendel. Bargeman. Lower quay.* And in the narrow column on the right, where the Register marks its dead: *Drowned. Flood Night.*
Emrys turned the pages back without a word, to *Fane, Ines*, and laid his finger in the same column. The same two words.

"Two," he said. "Both drowned. Both that night. Eleven lines faded in ten years, one at a time. Someone has been putting out the Flood Night dead like lamps." He unfolded his tally from inside his coat. "Ten blank lines left. Nine of them drowned. And one that matches nobody."
"The twelfth."
"The twelfth."
Ada looked at the little flame, and at Emrys, and opened her mouth. "The boy on the steps—"
Red flared over Pike's lantern, hot and sudden.
She shut her mouth.
Emrys watched her face. "You can't," he said.
"I can't."
"Then don't." He folded the tally away. "I would rather have you here."

When he had gone, she took the brown paper out of the drawer and found she could not remember the song her mother sang at the sink. She knew there had been one. She could see the window, the steam, the yellow gloves. No tune. No words.
*6. Mum's song. At the sink.*
She put Pike's lantern on the shop shelf, since there was no hearth shelf waiting for it, and sat with it until first bell.
The tower stairs rang under her boots. At the top the wind sang in the louvres, and Tobias sat on the top step beside the clock with the unfitted wheel in his lap, tapping. Three short, one long.
"I want to tell Odile," Ada said. "What your lantern showed me. The first time. All of it, the crack of timber too. Only with your leave."
Tobias tapped. "She'll hate me."
"Maybe."

"Ten years I've crossed the square to miss her." He scowled at the wheel. "Wound too tight. That's me." Tap, tap, tap, tap. "Tell her. And I'll stand there while you do. Half past too late for anything else."
Odile's front room was warm, and the stove ticked, and there were five cups on the table, one of them Ines's, going cold. The green dress stood on its dummy by the window, one sleeve on.
Tobias stood in the doorway with his hat in his hands and would not come further in.
"Odile," said Ada. "On Flood Night. What did Ines do?"
Odile took the pins out of her mouth. Slowly, as if she was reading it off the inside of her own head.

"She was at the window. Then she was out the door, no coat, shouting for the Vale boy. Little scrap from the lower quay, always on the steps with a bent pin, fishing for nothing." She almost smiled. "She'd have gone in after anybody's cat."
Emrys had gone very quiet. Quieter than Ada had ever heard him.
"I had a bent pin," he said.
Odile looked at him. At the buttoned coat, the careful hands, the face she had poured tea for at her own table.
"For the record," said Emrys, and stopped, and started again. "Someone pulled me out. I never knew who." His voice nearly went. "She went in for me."
Nobody said anything. The stove ticked.
"Tobias gave me leave," said Ada. "To tell you what his lantern holds."

And she told it, all of it, plainly: the dark quay, the water, a long splitting crack of timber overhead, Ines turning towards the sound, and Tobias's hands striking her, and Ines falling into the canal.
Odile's hand went to her pincushion and stayed there.

Emrys put his spectacles back on. "The hall keeps a wreck and salvage book," he said. "I read Flood Night yesterday. Ninth bell: the head beam of the lower sluice gave way and came down across the quay." He looked at the doorway. "Timber. Overhead. At ninth bell, on that quay, there is only one."
Odile turned, very slowly, to the man in the door.
"He pushed her out from under it," she said.
Tobias's fingers had been tapping on the door frame since he arrived. Three short, one long.
They stopped.
That night Odile would not let Ada go home.
She sat by the window with the dress across her knees and the lamp turned up. "I'm going to finish it," she said. "I can, now."
She set the second sleeve first, quick and neat. Then there was only the hem. Ines had pinned it, crooked as a dog's hind leg, and in ten years Odile had never touched it. It was hers.
Odile drew the pins out one by one and stuck them in the cushion on her wrist. Halfway along, her fingers stopped.
Something stiff inside the fold. A slip of paper, folded small, pinned through.
She unpinned it and opened it in the lamplight. At the top, in Ines's hand, a date. Odile did not need to say which.
She read it aloud, and her voice came out slower and lower than her own.
"If the lamps go dark tonight, don't blame the girl."
